newsitem.title: USA: Zaire force decision expected this week -Pentagon.
newsitem.headline: Zaire force decision expected this week -Pentagon.

text.p: Military officials from Canada, the United States and about a dozen other nations will meet in Germany on Thursday to assess the rapidly changing need for a humanitarian relief force in Zaire, the Pentagon said on Monday.

Representatives of nations that offered to send troops to support a U.N.-authorised relief effort in Zaire and possibly Rwanda will meet at U.S. European military headquarters in Stuttgart, said Pentagon spokeswoman Army Lt. Col. Nancy Burt.

"I expect something to come out on Thursday," she said, adding the meeting would be attended by Canadian Army Lt. Gen. Marice Baril, who has been designated to head a military task force to help refugees in Zaire.

Although tens of thousands of refugees in Zaire have returned to Rwanda in recent days, U.S. officials stressed privately there was still need for humanitarian relief for those remaining in Zaire. The question, they said, was how much military support would be needed to assure distribution of food and other aid either in Zaire or Rwanda.

The Washington Post reported in Tuesday's edition that senior U.S. officials had tentatively concluded the international security force proposed by Canada and approved by President Bill Clinton last week is no longer needed.
U.S. officials now believe there is no need for foreign troops to provide protection, since refugees are returning to Rwanda from eastern Zaire, the Post said.

Instead of 1,000 U.S. ground troops, smaller groups of American supply troops and cargo delivery teams would be sent to help civilian relief agencies distribute aid to refugees back in Rwanda, the newspaper said, quoting senior officials.
The meeting in Stuttgart, also to include representatives from Britain and France, will study a detailed report from military assessment teams already in Zaire and Rwanda.

Clinton last week tentatively offered 1,000 U.S. troops to move into Goma, Zaire, and another 2,000 or 3,000 support troops to be based in nearby countries. But Defence Secretary William Perry said over the weekend that the sudden flow of refugees home to Rwanda had changed the picture and that a decision would be made this week.
"I think every country (that has offered troops) has a different idea of what they want to do," said one Pentagon official, who asked not to be identified.

Pentagon officials said U.S. Air Force cargo planes and crews had already been moved to Moron Air Base in Spain to take part in a potential "air bridge" to central Africa and that other planes could be moved quickly to countries near Zaire after diplomatic arrangements are made.

At the State Department, spokesman Glyn Davies said a U.S. relief team in Rwanda was working with planners in Washington and U.S. diplomats elsewhere to determine how best to help the refugees, who he said were streaming back to Rwanda in a 40-mile (64 km) column.
Members of a U.S. Disaster Assistance Team reported that medical supplies were adequate and the World Food Programme has more than enough to feed the returning refugees, Davies said.
In addition, Davies said, returnees receive a 60-day food ration plus tools and seeds once they arrive at their home villages.

However, he said that international aid workers had not yet had access to some 350,000 Rwandans remaining in the so-called Great Lakes region of Zaire, and therefore it was difficult to know exactly how many refugees remained and how they were faring.
